tone.notes: First person, short sentences, light slang ("ridiculous", "One day here?"), Tilly's catchphrase once and a two-part rating as the closer. Casual, curious and honest; nothing mean. Fits a 13+ audience.

banned_topics.notes: Planetary science only. No people, deaths, violence, politics, religion or health advice; every fact is sourced to NASA, so nothing is made up. The keyword screen found nothing.

visuals.notes: Reviewed the 8 sampled frames plus extra frames at 2.2-4.0s, 18.5s, 24.3s, 26.5s, 27.8s, 29.0s and 34.5s. Code-drawn Jupiter on a dark starfield with a new view per fact, as the series promises; labels and captions are readable at phone size and inside the safe areas. The first render failed this check: in the tilt view the "3°" number sat on top of the "spin axis" label for the whole beat. The renderer's number position was fixed and the episode re-rendered; in this render the number sits clear above the label. Minor, not blocking: the angle counts up, so intermediate values (e.g. "1.4°") show for about a second before it lands on 3°; the "11 Earths wide" label is fully visible for under a second because the hook is short.

character.notes: Tilly is off screen (placement hidden) as the series requires. Lines match her file: discovers facts on the spot, "Okay, review time.", rating format "Size: five out of five. Landing spots: zero." The voice is the Kokoro af_heart setting from her file; the audio was checked by the automated loudness and caption-sync checks, not listened to by the reviewer.

learnings: The tilt view was first used here: for small tilts (a few degrees) the big angle number used to collide with the axis label; the renderer now lifts the number above the label, but check the tilt frame by eye on every planet.
The automated checks do not catch text overlapping other text; the reviewer must look for it in every view with two or more labels.
A two-view hook of about 4 seconds leaves the second view's label on screen for under a second; keep that label to three words or put the comparison in its own beat.
The Jupiter palette (6 tan and cream bands, glow #f0d9b5) reads clearly as Jupiter on the dark starfield.
When NASA pages disagree on a number (moon counts), leave the fact out rather than hedge; the episode did not miss it.
